node-1.label: Sudden onset pain and redness in the right eye, with photophobia

node-2.label: 83-year-old Caucasian male farmer, known for 3 months to have a hypermature cataract in the right eye and a mature cataract in the left eye, scheduled for cataract extraction in the left eye first followed by the right eye; no history of ocular trauma or previous ocular surgery; no relevant family history or ophthalmological conditions; not on any topical or systemic medication

node-3.label: During preoperative consultation for left eye cataract surgery, he reported acute ocular pain and photophobia in the right eye that began a few days prior

node-4.label: Clinical examination showed visual acuity of light perception in the right eye and counting fingers in the left eye; intraocular pressure was 50 mmHg in the right eye and 13 mmHg in the left eye; slit lamp biomicroscopy of the right eye revealed circumciliary congestion, diffuse corneal edema, pseudohypopyon, complete lens opacification, and suspended white particles in the anterior chamber and pupillary area

attrs.why: Both the pathologist and radiologist analyses converge on lens-induced glaucoma. The pathologist explicitly favors phacolytic glaucoma at 0.90, and the radiologist independently supports phacolytic glaucoma based on the hypermature cataract, high intraocular pressure, pseudohypopyon, corneal edema, photophobia, and hyper-reflective vitreous band. This independent agreement strengthens the umbrella diagnosis of lens-induced glaucoma, so confidence is increased from 0.90 to 0.95.

Although the hypermature cataract and anterior chamber findings can fit lens-induced uveitis, the pathologist considers lens-induced uveitis less likely than phacolytic glaucoma, and the B-scan hyper-reflective vitreous band is more consistent with lens-related inflammation/macrophage response. Confidence reduced from 0.55 to 0.40.

The pathologist notes that angle-closure glaucoma lacks trauma or surgery and that the hypermature cataract is atypical; the acute pain and high intraocular pressure are better explained by lens-induced glaucoma. Confidence reduced from 0.25 to 0.15.

The pathologist notes that infectious endophthalmitis lacks trauma or surgery and is less favored; the pseudohypopyon and white particles are more consistent with lens-induced inflammation than infection. Confidence reduced from 0.10 to 0.05.
